entries.title: Music that moves with Mario
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: How can a tune help a player read a moving game?
body: Koji Kondo describes the original Super Mario Bros. score as a set of practical responses to the screen. The open ground, underwater passages, underground rooms and castle needed different musical identities. Limited sound resources did not make these locations interchangeable. A player could hear a change in surroundings as well as see it. That is a useful starting point for listening: compare the pace and texture of two locations before trying to name a favourite tune. The score helps divide a continuous adventure into situations with different expectations.

In his 2023 Library of Congress interview, Kondo explains that the Ground Theme combines evenly divided melody and bass parts with a differently divided percussion rhythm. He recalls finding that relationship by trying an idea rather than following a fixed formula. The result can be approached as a small arrangement of moving parts. Listen first to the melody, then to the accompaniment, then to their overlap. The music has forward motion without requiring every sound to strike together. Its apparent simplicity contains several kinds of timing working at once.

The same interview places music beside the game's changing conditions. Kondo describes short sounds for failure and success, and music that accelerates when little time remains. These are different jobs from establishing the atmosphere of a location. One marks an outcome; another changes the urgency of an action still in progress. Heard this way, the score is also part of the information available to the player. A familiar melody can remain recognisable while its function changes, turning listening into another way of knowing what is happening on screen.

In 2023 the Ground Theme entered the United States National Recording Registry, the first game recording selected for that collection. The work being recognised dates to 1985, while the archival decision belongs to a much later moment. Keeping those dates separate matters. A game tune can be heard during repeated play, then in arrangements and other settings, and eventually studied as a recording in its own right. The registry does not replace the original game context. It gives listeners another route back to the relationship between a tune, a machine and an action.

entries.title: The recording session behind an island
entries.event_semantics: 29 May 1997 is the dated recording session in the archival record, not Riven’s release.
entries.article_question: What can one surviving production tape tell us about making Riven?
body: A surviving record in the Video Game History Foundation catalogue identifies a Riven ADR recording session on 29 May 1997. The carrier is Betacam SP, and the tape bears the working label Myst II Audio Session. This is a production event, not the game's release date. Even before the footage is examined, the record places a particular piece of audio work inside the making of Riven. An island that appears remote and self-contained on screen also depended on scheduled sessions, recording equipment and material that could be kept, labelled and later catalogued.

The wider Cyan collection includes raw camera footage, composite tests, developer interviews and behind-the-scenes material associated with Riven. Those categories describe different stages of production. A filmed performance is not yet the final image inside a game, and a composite test is evidence of a process rather than necessarily a scene players encountered. Bringing the categories together changes the question asked of an archive. Instead of only asking what the finished island looked like, we can ask which experiments, performances and technical steps helped make that appearance possible.

The item record warns that this footage overlaps another ADR-session video in the collection. Two catalogue entries therefore do not automatically mean two different sessions or twice as much independent evidence. The distinction is small but important when reconstructing production history. We should compare what each object contains before deciding how they relate. The record alone also does not identify every speaker or establish what was said. That work requires viewing and describing the material, with permissions and uncertainty recorded alongside any conclusions drawn from it.

Cyan's 2024 account of revisiting Riven describes a reimagining, with changed puzzles, expanded narrative and movement through the scenes. Project manager Ryan Warzecha also names discussions involving members of the original team and consultation with Robyn Miller. That later work is valuable evidence of a return, but it must not silently stand in for 1997. A modern screenshot and an original recording session answer different questions. Read together, they show how a studio can revisit a world while its earlier production materials retain their own dates, methods and historical value.

entries.title: Scoring a meeting between strangers
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: How do musical scale and performance support Journey’s small social encounter?
body: Before Journey's release, Austin Wintory described its music as intimate overall, despite the large scale suggested by a distant mountain and a heroic journey. That decision offers a useful way into the score. Musical size need not simply copy the size of the landscape. A small gesture can draw attention towards the traveller within it, while a larger passage can arrive as a change rather than a constant condition. Wintory's account presents the score as an emotional arc, with proportion and contrast doing work that volume alone cannot do.

Jenova Chen's release announcement describes Journey as an anonymous online adventure that can be travelled alone or with a stranger. The destination is shared, but the encounter is not introduced through a conventional conversation. Against that premise, waiting or continuing becomes something another person can notice. Music belongs to this setting of limited explicit explanation. It can support a passage without telling us exactly what a companion thinks. The distinction preserves the encounter's uncertainty: the other figure is a participant moving through the same place, not a feeling the soundtrack can conclusively explain.

Wintory's album notes put the musicians near the centre of the story. Tina Guo's cello appears alongside flute, harp, viola, serpent, voice and orchestral players. The credits also distinguish composition, production, orchestration, programming and recording work. These are not interchangeable contributions. Listening for the cello's phrasing, or for the change between an individual instrument and an ensemble, gives the performance a place in the article. It also prevents an orchestral game score from being described as if it emerged fully formed from a single person's software.

The composer-hosted album page carries a 2013 release date while crediting the 2012 score. The game itself was announced for March 2012. These dates identify different publications, and neither should be used to erase the other. An album also fixes an order in which tracks can be heard outside the player's changing pace. Comparing that listening sequence with the game's movement is an editorial invitation, not a claim that they behave identically. The music can be valued as a recording while its original task remains connected to a journey someone was taking.

entries.title: A camera makes the future visible
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: What changes when a dystopian game asks the player to photograph rather than fight?
body: Umurangi Generation places a camera in the player's hands and gives them photographic work in Tauranga, Aotearoa. Its official description identifies the player as a courier for the Tauranga Express, with lenses and equipment becoming available along the way. The action is therefore organised around looking, framing and making an image. A location can hold several possible photographs rather than a single target. This changes how an urban scene is approached: distance, angle and what fits inside the frame become practical decisions, made through a familiar tool.

ACMI describes the game through Māori science fiction, climate crisis and militarised responses to disaster. It identifies Mauao, visible from the first level, as significant to the Ngāi Te Rangi people of creator Naphtali Faulkner. That specificity matters more than a generic description of neon city streets. The setting is not an interchangeable future metropolis. Its viewpoint connects a particular place and maker to the things the player is asked to notice. The museum record supports that context without turning Māori experience into a substitute for every Indigenous perspective.

ACMI also records Faulkner's photograph of his family home after the Black Summer fires reached Lismore in 2019. The physical print has its own object identifier and collection status. Beside the fictional city, it supplies a different kind of evidence: a dated photograph connected to the maker's life rather than an illustration created for the game. The two images should not be collapsed into one literal story. They can instead be read in relation, with clear captions that distinguish a real damaged home from a designed science-fiction setting.

The official game page says photographs are assessed for colour, content and composition, with their cash value contributing to the final payout. That gives looking both an expressive and a practical role. A photograph is something the player makes, but it also enters the game's system of evaluation. The interesting tension is not that a number can settle what a picture means. It is that the same environment supports a task, a composition and an act of attention. The player chooses what to include while the world continues beyond the edges of the image.

entries.title: When an image becomes a path
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: How does Monument Valley turn an optical illusion into a rule the player can use?
body: Monument Valley introduces Ida through architecture that cannot always be understood as ordinary physical space. Ustwo's description emphasises hidden paths, changing monuments and optical illusions. Those elements make the image part of the puzzle rather than a backdrop behind it. A staircase or connection has to be read in the view presented to the player. The interesting action is often a change in understanding: a route that did not seem usable becomes available when the structure is reconsidered. Looking at the composition is already part of learning how to move through it.

A small figure makes the architecture legible as somewhere to travel. Ustwo's premise is not simply to display impossible monuments, but to guide Ida through them. That relationship gives an abstract arrangement a practical measure. A ledge is wide enough to stand on; a passage is something to reach; a change in the structure can open a way forward. The figure does not need to dominate the composition for these relationships to matter. Its position asks a concrete question of the picture: where can this traveller go from here?

Ustwo's tenth-anniversary material places the game's first iOS launch in 2014 and includes a photograph of the team celebrating an App Store feature. That image supplies something the finished monuments do not: a view of the people around the work. It should retain its date and occasion rather than becoming an anonymous photograph of game development. The distinction also keeps the article grounded. The carefully composed world had a production setting, and the studio's later recollection is evidence of how that team chose to remember its reception.

The developer's 2024 anniversary post looks back to the 3 April 2014 iOS release, while the anniversary timeline separately identifies the later Panoramic Edition. These are different moments in a work's life. A wider modern presentation should not silently stand in for the framing of the original mobile edition. For this exhibit, the useful comparison is specific: how much of the structure is visible, where Ida sits within it, and how the path is presented. Later editions can help us study those choices, provided their identities remain clear in every image and caption.

cards.heading: A route inside the picture
cards.body: Monument Valley introduces Ida through architecture that cannot always be understood as ordinary physical space. Ustwo's description emphasises hidden paths, changing monuments and optical illusions. Those elements make the image part of the puzzle rather than a backdrop behind it. A staircase or connection has to be read in the view presented to the player. The interesting action is often a change in understanding: a route that did not seem usable becomes available when the structure is reconsidered. Looking at the composition is already part of learning how to move through it.

cards.heading: Ida gives the structure a scale
cards.body: A small figure makes the architecture legible as somewhere to travel. Ustwo's premise is not simply to display impossible monuments, but to guide Ida through them. That relationship gives an abstract arrangement a practical measure. A ledge is wide enough to stand on; a passage is something to reach; a change in the structure can open a way forward. The figure does not need to dominate the composition for these relationships to matter. Its position asks a concrete question of the picture: where can this traveller go from here?

The carefully composed world had a production setting, and the studio's later recollection is evidence of how that team chose to remember its reception.

entries.title: The small allowances inside a difficult jump
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: How can a demanding platform game make an imperfect input count?
body: Maddy Thorson's account of Celeste describes several allowances around apparently exact movement. A jump can still count briefly after leaving an edge, and an early button press can be remembered until landing. These windows help an intended action reach the screen even when its timing is imperfect. Thorson explicitly places the techniques in a wider history rather than claiming to have invented them. The interesting distinction is between a precise result and an unforgiving input. A difficult route can demand practice while allowing the player a little room to express what they meant.

Celeste's changelog records Dash Assist as an addition in version 1.3.1.0. Version 1.4.0.0 expanded control bindings and offered different ways of operating the grab action. Those entries make assistance a history of specific revisions, rather than a single feature that never changed after launch. They also invite a practical comparison: adjusting the timing of a move is different from changing how a button is held. Both can affect whether a route is usable without requiring the museum to assume that all players need the same adjustment.

An earlier update changed the wording of Celeste's pause menus: returning to the map or restarting a chapter no longer appeared under a submenu called Give Up. The same changelog credits community feedback when revising the Assist Mode description. These are changes to language, not to the shape of a platform, but they alter the way a choice is presented. A menu can describe an action without passing judgement on the person choosing it. The record makes that editorial decision visible as part of the game's continuing design work.

Noel Berry's public Celeste repository includes selected source files as a learning resource. It offers a different kind of evidence from a finished gameplay recording: readers can inspect some of the implementation behind the movement. The distinction between code and the commercial game's other materials remains important. The repository's licence is not a licence to redistribute every image, sound or level in Celeste. Used within its stated scope, the material connects a discussion of game feel to authored technical work, while keeping a small code release separate from the complete game.

entries.title: How a paperwork game learns to make mistakes
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: What had to be balanced before checking documents could become Papers, Please?
body: In his February 2013 development notes, Lucas Pope discusses introducing the game's concepts gradually and balancing incorrect documents against legitimate entrants. This is also a production problem. If every visitor has an obvious fault, checking stops feeling like a decision. If the rules arrive too quickly, the player may not understand what they are being asked to inspect. The notes show Pope arranging the conditions under which an error can be meaningful, rather than simply adding more paperwork to make a border checkpoint seem complicated.

An April entry identifies a counterintuitive balancing problem: putting more errors into one entrant's documents can make the inspection easier, because the player only needs to notice one of them. Difficulty does not rise neatly with the quantity of wrong information. A single subtle mismatch may demand more attention than several obvious contradictions. The observation shifts the discussion from the appearance of a crowded desk to the logic of a decision. What matters is the evidence needed for a verdict, and how readily a person working under pressure can find it.

Pope's April log also records a discussion of pixels and vectors after feedback around the Game Developers Conference. He considered the presentation and retained pixel art. That is more informative than describing the finished look as an automatic consequence of working alone or making a small game. Visual form was open to discussion during production. A useful question is how marks, names and document edges remain readable at the desk. The development record lets us examine that question without inventing a reason for every visual choice.

In February, Pope described native Windows and Mac builds with the first five days roughed out, while night screens were still unfinished and some systems were not yet exposed to the player. That snapshot is valuable precisely because it is incomplete. A mechanic can exist in code before it has a finished interface or a place in the player's day. Reading the log in sequence reveals a work being assembled and tested. It also prevents an early screenshot from being treated as proof that the final game's whole structure was already settled.

entries.title: The artist between a drawing and a display
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: What does remaking early Final Fantasy pixel art reveal about its original making?
body: Kazuko Shibuya recalls redrawing the first Final Fantasy's prologue landscape as silhouettes to fit limited memory. The picture appeared when the player crossed the bridge; it was not an unused scene. When she recreated it for Pixel Remaster, the original digital data was unavailable. A printout she had kept supplied a reference. This makes preservation tangible. A paper copy of released artwork helped its original artist return to earlier decisions. The surviving sheet and the later redraw belong to different moments, and both need clear dates and captions.

In the same interview, Shibuya discusses how colour behaved on older cathode-ray-tube displays, in contrast with the sharply separated pixels of modern screens. Redrawing an early character is therefore not just a matter of counting squares. The display is part of how neighbouring colours become an image. This gives the remaster an artistic problem rather than a simple instruction to make everything sharper. A comparison should identify both the edition and the viewing conditions, so the museum does not confuse a modern enlargement with the appearance of the original hardware.

Koichi Ishii's account of the first Final Fantasy describes a production arrangement involving Shibuya, Takashi Tokita and himself. While Shibuya was occupied with other work, Tokita helped Ishii learn the sprite tools, and Ishii worked on the side-view battle presentation. Such recollections complicate a convenient single-artist story. A recognisable character can pass through design, tool learning, input and revision before it reaches the screen. The interview makes those handovers worth naming. Crediting Shibuya's contribution does not require assigning every early Final Fantasy pixel to her alone.

Square Enix's Pixel Remaster FAQ identifies Shibuya with the redrawn character graphics and describes an effort to keep the feel of the earlier games. It separately identifies the illustration galleries and Yoshitaka Amano's concept art. Those distinctions matter when different kinds of art appear together in one exhibit. A concept illustration, an original sprite and a later redraw are related objects, not interchangeable versions of a single file. The 2021 project gives the museum a reason to compare them while preserving the authorship and date of each contribution.

entries.article_question: How does Rez connect a player action to music, and what changed when its creators returned?
body: Adam Freeland's account of making Fear for Rez describes a task unlike delivering a finished track to play unchanged. The developers needed parts they could loop and layer as the level unfolded, and he also supplied sounds for events such as explosions. Music and interaction were being prepared for one another. Compare a recorded arrangement: the same musical material has to remain coherent while a game decides when particular events occur. This is a production method, not a claim that every player hears an identical sequence.

The participants' retrospective also describes the timing of shots and explosions in relation to the music. An action is made audible inside an arrangement rather than placed arbitrarily over it. That relationship gives a simple shooting gesture another dimension: it has a visual result and a musical position. Listening to an authorised recording alongside an official gameplay example can make the distinction clear. It does not prove that a particular emotional response is universal. The historical claim is narrower and more useful: sound effects were designed to work with the track's timing and key.

Writing before Rez Infinite's 2016 release, Tetsuya Mizuguchi described Area X as an experiment rather than merely a higher-resolution copy of an old level. His account emphasises trying ideas, discarding what did not work and building a different visual and playable form. That return changes the terms of comparison. Classic Rez and Area X can share an interest in linked sound and action while looking and moving differently. The exhibit should make those differences visible, instead of allowing a modern particle scene to stand silently for the original 2001 game.

Mizuguchi's later account explicitly thanks development partners Monstars and Resonair for bringing Area X to life, alongside Sony's support. Naming those contributions keeps a discussion of a creative director connected to the people and organisations making the work. The same publication provides directly captured PlayStation 4 Pro images and identifies their hardware. Those captions are useful evidence, not a licence to call every image of Rez an original Dreamcast capture. Production credits and image provenance answer different questions, and a careful exhibit needs both when comparing the work across editions.

cards.heading: The return had a team behind it
cards.body: Mizuguchi's later account explicitly thanks development partners Monstars and Resonair for bringing Area X to life, alongside Sony's support. Naming those contributions keeps a discussion of a creative director connected to the people and organisations making the work. The same publication provides directly captured PlayStation 4 Pro images and identifies their hardware. Those captions are useful evidence, not a licence to call every image of Rez an original Dreamcast capture. Production credits and image provenance answer different questions, and a careful exhibit needs both when comparing the work across editions.

entries.title: Two voices inside Bastion
entries.event_semantics: Year anchors the work discussed; this is not a birth, publication-calendar slot or assumed worldwide release date.
entries.article_question: What do the soundtrack credits reveal beyond the name of a composer?
body: Bastion's official soundtrack credits Darren Korb with writing, producing and recording its music, but they identify vocal performances separately. Ashley Barrett sings Build That Wall, while Korb sings Mother, I'm Here. The distinction lets a listener follow people as well as melodies. A composer's name on an album does not mean that the same person performed every sound it contains. Starting with the individual credits gives the songs a clearer human setting and makes room for the different work involved in writing a piece, recording it and singing it.

The album credits bring Barrett and Korb together on Setting Sail, Coming Home. Other entries distinguish lyrics by Greg Kasavin and performances by Logan Cunningham. These details resist a shorthand in which one celebrated name absorbs everyone else's contribution. They also suggest a useful listening route: move between a solo vocal and the shared performance, paying attention to how the voices occupy the arrangement. That comparison is an invitation to hear the recording, not a claim about an undocumented studio session. No song lyric needs to be reproduced to make its authorship visible.

Supergiant's description of Bastion places a reactive narrator beside its action role-playing structure and the work of building a refuge. That spoken presence belongs to the same game as the songs, but it has a different job. One responds to an unfolding action; the album presents fixed recordings with their own performers and credits. Keeping the forms distinct helps an exhibit discuss voice without reducing it to a single category. A visitor can compare narration, a sung phrase and an instrumental passage while asking what each one makes available to the player.

In March 2012, Greg Kasavin announced guitar and piano arrangements of four Bastion songs after requests from listeners. These sheets offered another way to encounter the music: through a playable arrangement rather than only a recording. The date belongs to that later publication, not to the game's original launch. Nor does a freely offered arrangement automatically grant permission to redistribute every page or performance. The announcement is useful evidence of a specific response to an audience, connecting a game's soundtrack to people who wanted to make the music with their own hands.
